newsitem.title: MEXICO: Guatemala refugees will stay in Mexico despite peace.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala refugees will stay in Mexico despite peace.

text.p: Thousands of Guatemalan refugees, who have spent almost 15 years in Mexico to escape bloodshed back home, will not return despite the imminent prospect of peace, a top refugee official said on Wednesday.

Michel Gabaudan, head of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees in Mexico, said in an interview that up to 23,000 of the 30,000 Guatemalan refugees in Mexico were expected to remain, taking advantage of Mexican moves to offer them eventual citizenship.

In Oslo, Norway, on Wednesday the Guatemalan government and leftist guerrillas signed a ceasefire agreement that was the first of three key accords expected to lead to the official conclusion of the 36-year war on Dec. 29.

Refugees, many with long-held sympathies for the rebel struggle, still suffer trauma from the massacres and right-wing repression that drove them across the border to Mexico during the height of Guatemala's conflict in the early 1980s. Some 140,000 have died or "disappeared" in the war.

But Gabaudan, a Frenchman who has spent years working with Guatemala's mosty indigenous refugees, said that for the most part they were not staying away because of fears of a resurgence of violence, or doubts about the peace process, but simply because they had made their homes elsewhere.
He noted that many returned when there were no prospects of peace in the early 1990s.

"The reason most refugees ... do not go back is not because of security fears. It is basically because they have made their lives here. There are still violations of human rights (in Guatemala), though clearly not anymore (because of) government policy. People who don't go back want to stay because they are better off here."
In a bid to help Guatemala's peace process, the Mexican government has agreed to give legal status to non-returnees.
Next week, Gabaudan said, Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo was scheduled to hand out the full rights of citizenship to some Guatemalan refugees in a ceremony in Mexico City.
Most of those who will benefit immediately are in almost self-sufficent refugee camps in the southeastern states of Campeche and Quintana Roo, Gabaudan said.
In Chiapas state, which borders Guatemala and has a smouldering rebel and land distribution problem of its own, the process is expected to take longer.
